newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Labour laws cost Australian jobs -survey.
newsitem.headline: Labour laws cost Australian jobs -survey.

text.p: A survey issued on Friday backed suspicions that Australia's unfair dismissal laws had suppressed full-time employment growth.

"Eight-point-eight percent of companies surveyed said they had employed fewer permanent staff, or had deferred plans to employ permanent staff, as a direct consequence of the unfair dismissal legislation contained in the Industrial Relations Reform Act (of 1993)," job agency Recruitment Solutions reported from its survey of 750 companies.
Australia has failed in recent years to achieve sustainable growth in full-time jobs.
March data issued on Tuesday showed that current full-time employment is now only 10,000 higher than a pre-recession peak recorded seven years ago.

In 1993, the former Labor government greatly limited employers' ability to shed staff with laws designed to prevent unfair dismissal -- a move which critics said made employers less likely to hire new staff.

Prime Minister John Howard's new Liberal-National government diluted those laws late last year but business leaders and some economists have said that even the new system was still holding down employment.
Recruitment Solutions' survey found that 13 percent of employers had turned to temporary staff to avoid Labor's legislation.
"These figures provide the strongest evidence that the legislation is not achieving what it set out to achieve," the agency's executive director, Greg Savage, said in a statement.
"Certainly the recent changes by the Howard government are positive, but they don't go far enough."
